items.title: The Phoebus cartel
items.claim: In 1924 major light bulb manufacturers met in Geneva and agreed to limit bulb lifetimes. From what figure to what?
items.reveal:
The Phoebus cartel (Osram, Philips, GE and others) coordinated lower lifetime targets and tested members' compliance.

The cartel dissolved by 1939 but the case remains a foundational example of planned obsolescence in design history.
items.why: Designed lifespans are choices, not inevitabilities of materials or physics.

items.title: Rams's ten principles
items.claim: How many principles did Dieter Rams set out for 'good design' while at Braun in the 1970s?
items.reveal_title: Ten principles ending with 'good design is as little design as possible'
items.reveal:
Rams's principles include innovative, useful, aesthetic, understandable, unobtrusive, honest, long-lasting, thorough, environmentally friendly, and as little design as possible.

Apple designers including Jony Ive have publicly cited their influence.
items.why: Many contemporary product aesthetics descend from one designer's deliberate articulation of values.

items.title: How long the Bauhaus lasted
items.claim: The Bauhaus, founded by Walter Gropius in 1919, was closed by the Nazi government in 1933. How many years did it operate?
items.reveal:
The school ran in Weimar (1919-1925), Dessau (1925-1932) and Berlin (1932-1933). Faculty including Albers, Breuer, Mies van der Rohe and Moholy-Nagy emigrated, spreading the curriculum to Chicago, Harvard and beyond.

The Bauhaus's influence on global design vastly outlasted its institutional life.
items.why: Some of the most influential schools in design history were short-lived experiments.

items.title: Morris's contradiction
items.claim: William Morris's Arts and Crafts movement (founded 1860s) argued for handmade goods accessible to all. What was the tension critics identified?

options.text: Handmade goods proved expensive, reaching mostly affluent buyers

items.reveal:
Morris & Co. produced wallpaper, textiles and furniture at prices that mostly the prosperous middle classes could afford. Morris himself recognised the contradiction.

The movement nonetheless reshaped expectations of designed everyday objects.
items.why: Design movements often struggle with the economics of their own ideals.

items.title: The first fully synthetic plastic
items.claim: Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, was patented in which year?
items.reveal:
Baekeland's phenol-formaldehyde resin enabled mass-produced radio housings, telephones, and electrical insulators.

Global plastic production has grown from negligible amounts in 1950 to roughly 400 million tonnes per year by the 2020s.
items.why: Material innovations enable design categories that did not exist before.

items.title: Cradle to Cradle
items.claim: Cradle to Cradle (2002) by William McDonough and Michael Braungart argued for what shift in design thinking?

options.text: Design products so materials cycle back as technical or biological nutrients

items.reveal_title: Materials as nutrients in cycles, not waste streams
items.reveal:
The book distinguishes 'technical' cycles (industrial materials recovered indefinitely) from 'biological' cycles (materials safely returning to ecosystems).

The approach informs current discussions of the circular economy and EU eco-design regulations.
items.why: Design intent at the material-choice stage shapes what is possible at end of life.

items.title: Fitts's law
items.claim: Paul Fitts's 1954 model predicts the time to point at a target. What variables does it use?

options.text: Colour and brightness of the target
Distance to target and target width
Number of fingers and finger length

items.reveal_title: Movement time depends on distance over width
items.reveal:
Fitts's law: MT = a + b * log2(2D/W). The model still informs button sizing in user interfaces and the design of touchscreen targets.

Apple Human Interface Guidelines minimum 44pt touch targets descend from this lineage.
items.why: Quantitative models from the 1950s still shape decisions in modern UI design.

items.title: Norman doors
items.claim: Don Norman's The Design of Everyday Things (1988) gave its name to which everyday failure?

options.text: Doors that signal push when they should pull

items.reveal_title: When the handle says one thing and the door does another
items.reveal:
Norman argued affordances and signifiers should match action. A vertical bar suggests pulling; a flat plate suggests pushing.

The book is on standard reading lists for product design and HCI courses.
items.why: Bad design often fails by promising one action while requiring another.

items.title: iPod numbers
items.claim: Apple launched the iPod on 23 October 2001. About how many units were ultimately sold across the product line by 2014?
items.reveal:
Apple's quarterly disclosures by 2014 totalled around 390 million iPods. The platform created cultural and commercial conditions for the iPhone.

The last iPod model (iPod touch) was discontinued in 2022.
items.why: A product can transform an industry without remaining a category leader forever.

items.title: Riveted jeans patent
items.claim: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented riveted denim trousers. In which year?
items.reveal:
Davis, a Nevada tailor, had the rivet idea; Strauss provided the cloth and patent capital. The trouser was a workwear product for miners and labourers for most of its first century.

Global denim production now exceeds 7 billion pairs per year.
items.why: A small mechanical detail can define a category for over 150 years.

items.title: Female crash-test dummies
items.claim: Standard crash-test dummies are based on male physiology. When was a regulated female-sized dummy widely required in US tests?

options.text: Female-sized dummies were not required in US frontal crash tests until 2003 and a fully biofidelic female dummy is still under development

items.reveal_title: Required test dummies under-represented women for decades
items.reveal:
Caroline Criado Perez (Invisible Women, 2019) and NHTSA documents show female-sized dummies only became required in some US frontal tests from 2003, and a more biofidelic THOR-AV female dummy is still being developed.

Women face higher serious-injury risk in comparable crashes.
items.why: Standardised testing reflects the assumptions of its designers and reshapes downstream safety for those left out.

items.title: How long aseptic milk lasts
items.claim: Tetra Pak's aseptic packaging (developed in Sweden in the 1950s-60s) allows long ambient storage. How long can typical UHT milk stay unopened at room temperature?
items.reveal_title: Half a year or more without refrigeration
items.reveal:
UHT-treated milk in aseptic cartons typically keeps for 6 to 9 months sealed at ambient temperature. This transformed dairy supply chains in countries with weak cold storage.

The packaging itself combines paper, polymer and aluminium layers.
items.why: A packaging innovation can change which products are commercially viable in which regions.
